title: Managed hosting
summary: Configure the artifact, assigned port and external services before releasing the application.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Deploy Spring Boot App on Heroku: Easy Guide for Beginners

richText: Run an application on managed hosting
Managed hosting supplies an environment for the application process.
Choose a supported Java runtime and provide the packaged application.
The host’s build and start commands must match the project and generated artifact.
Bind the application to the port assigned by the platform.
Store credentials in the host’s configuration or secret system.

example.title: Start a JAR with a classic Heroku Procfile
description: This example uses Heroku’s classic Procfile process model. Other platforms and Heroku runtime generations can use different deployment settings.
Put the server setting in application.properties and the web command in a file named Procfile at the project root.
example.code:
# application.properties
server.port=${PORT:8080}

# Procfile
web: java -jar target/journal.jar
explanation: PORT is supplied by the host. The property falls back to 8080 locally.
web names the process that receives HTTP requests.
The JAR path must match the file produced by the build.
Use the current host documentation for its build and release procedure.

richText: Keep data outside a temporary application filesystem
Some hosts replace or clear the application filesystem during restart or deployment.
Use a persistent database for application data. Use persistent object storage for uploaded files.
For MongoDB Atlas, create a database user and configure network access for the host.
A database URI provides connection information. It does not open firewall or network access.
Record the application revision and configuration released to the host.
Read build logs to check packaging. Read process and application logs to check startup.
Confirm the process listens on the required port and the public endpoint responds.
Check an authenticated API request and a database read/write using controlled data.
Expect the platform to restart or stop processes. Handle shutdown and avoid duplicate effects when work is retried.
Keep a prior artifact for rollback. Replacing the JAR does not reverse a database migration or restore deleted data.
